Prologue: Actuality and Illusion in the Psychoanalytic Encounter

Gail Reed Issue Editor and Howard Levine Issue Editor

Howard Levine

Howard Levine  

The interrelation between actuality and illusion within the clinical encounter is a subject that has influenced the theory and practice of psychoanalysis since its beginnings, particularly with regard to how clinicians identify and construe the transference.

After he revised his theory in terms of psychic reality and the Oedipus complex, Freud continued to focus theoretical attention away from the pathogenic actuality or event to the illusion, or unconscious fantasy linked to phase-specific unconscious wishes. There is ample evidence of his ongoing clinical concern with the objective event as well as with the subjective meaning to which it gave rise (Freud, 1918; Kardiner, 1977; Levine, 1990). Despite that evidence, after Freud's death the idea that meaning developed from the reciprocal relation between inner and outer event was in practice often ignored in favor of a simplified version of fantasy so that there was more than a kernel of truth in the charge that classical psychoanalysis—as opposed to some classical analysts—did not pay sufficient attention to actual traumatic childhood events and their impact on the individual.

In retrospect, it is curious that a dichotomous relationship between actuality and illusion became so entrenched.

The Analyst's Experience in the Psychoanalytic Situation: A Continuum Between Objective and Subjective Reality

Alan Skolnikoff MD

Alan Skolnikoff

205 Edgewood Avenue
San Francisco, CA 94117

Alan Skolnikoff  

Traditionally, when we have described strong feelings in psychoanalysis or psychoanalytically oriented therapy, our reference has been to the patient's capacity to experience these emotions in relation to the analyst. In contrast, the more recent psychoanalytic literature (Schlesinger, 1981; Tyson, 1986; Skolnikoff, in press) has begun to focus on the complexities of the analyst's emotional experience with the patient. In the present paper, I offer an outline for a continuum between objective and subjective reality in the analyst's perception of the patient. Through clinical example, I will attempt to illustrate the complexity of the analyst's emotional reactions, their influence on and reflection of the analyst's (often unconscious) perception of the patient, and the therapeutic value of carefully studying these reactions.

If we begin with the assumption that the analyst is as much an emotional participant in the analytic process as is the patient, then the concept of psychic reality applies to the analyst's thoughts and behavior as well as to those of the patient. Our recognition of this expanded field will have consequences for our clinical theory and for analytic technique.

Dr. Skolnikoff is Training and Supervising Analyst, San Francisco Psychoanalytic Institute. He is Associate Clinical Professor, University of California, San Francisco.

Epilogue

Herbert Schlesinger PHD

Herbert Schlesinger

Herbert Schlesinger  

How do these articles affect our understanding of the role of the gender of patient and analyst in psychoanalytic practice? As the Prologue to this collection has detailed, not only feminists but critics of psychoanalysis, largely from outside the main stream (Horney, 1926; Thompson, 1942; Mitchell, 1974; Chodorow, 1989), have often singled out the one-sidedness of psychoanalytic theorizing. In its praxis, as well as in its theory of psychic development, psychoanalysis has been phallocentric. The major traditional theorists about the course of development, about the analytic situation, and about the quality of human experience have assumed the male as the norm, and only later, if at all, derived what ought to be the experience of the female by extension, exception, or modification. Occasional “insiders” (Deutsch, 1944, 1945; Kestenberg, 1968; Chasseguet-Smirgel, 1970; Schafer, 1974; Stoller, 1977, 1985; Bergman, 1982) have conceded the main points of criticism and have sought ways to accommodate them by revising various of the theories, altering some major dimensions and basic assumptions. One could say that this collection leaves the present unsatisfactory situation largely undisturbed. That is to say, it contains no single finding that would force a basic change in any central theory. But that would be a demanding standard to meet.

These thoughtful and well-selected papers will, however, require the serious reader to reconsider his or her own position with regard to several notions that have been passed on across generations and have, through repetition, attained the status of revealed truth, though with little in the way of empirical support and, interestingly, also with little apparent theoretical necessity.

The Analyst as Prince of Serendip

Elaine Cotlove

Elaine Cotlove

5415 West Cedar Lane
Suite 208B
Bethesda, MD 20814

Elaine Cotlove  

The title of this essay derives from a very old folktale about “The Three Princes of Serendip” (ancient Ceylon), who set forth to save their father's kingdom from the menace of dragons. On their journey, each found treasures which he had neither sought nor anticipated. From this tale Horace Walpole (1717-1797) coined the word serendipity.

How does the analytic work shape the analyst? Let me begin as we all begin: “What comes to mind …?”

For me, analytic work is at once my liberal education, my magic carpet, and my version of time travel. It can indeed be tedious and frustrating, but it can also be exceedingly colorful. I become an intimate participant in lives very different from mine, in place of origin, cultural priorities and expectations, and styles of perception and of coping. I have trouble reading novels anymore unless they are essentially autobiographical or exquisitely written; they don't hold a candle to the vividness and authenticity of what I hear in my office.

The couch itself is my time machine. One of my patients once aptly described herself as a station wagon, with all her past selves rattling around in the back, and she, as driver, having both to steer and to keep order. Sometimes past selves emerge on my couch in all but palpable form, perhaps not exactly as they once were, but certainly not as any adult could ever consciously recreate them.

Dr. Cotlove is Clinical Professor of Psychiatry, George Washington University Medical Center; she is on the Faculty of the Washington Psychoanalytic Institute.

Epilogue: Actuality, Illusion, and Clinical Authority

Gail Reed Issue Editor

Gail Reed

1199 Park Avenue
New York, NY 10128

Gail Reed  

Probably no clinical situation brings questions of actuality and illusion into clearer focus than the white heat of a transference neurosis and the common though much less talked about reciprocal “countertransference neurosis,” which both impedes the former's resolution and is often the material out of which the transference iatrogenically fashions itself. Skolnikoff writes aptly that intersubjectivity and more than transitory identification of analyst with patient is an often unacknowledged aspect of psychoanalytic processes. Yet even in the throes of such turmoil, all clinicians operate with the necessity that the patient hear some of the analyst's words, some of the time, as illuminating his or her transference illusion, rather than as only belonging to it, and that the analyst conduct himself to make this a possibility for the patient.

All our contributors comment on an aspect of providing this necessity. To see their commentaries in context, let us consider some clinical material, selected precisely because it demonstrates a low-grade but significant countertransference interference that, at the time of the sessions presented, had not been recognized by the analyst who later reported it to me. This interference reflects the powerful way in which the analytic process has been deeply engaged by both analyst and analysand and illustrates the inevitable, reciprocal, and reverberating effects of transference and countertransference forces on the unfolding process. Dedication

Joseph Lichtenberg Editor-in-Chief

Joseph Lichtenberg

Joseph Lichtenberg  

At the suggestion of the Issue Editors and with the enthusiastic agreement of the Psychoanalytic Inquiry editorial board, this issue is dedicated to Nathaniel London, M.D., 1927-1989.

Nat London and I grew up a few blocks apart in a neighborhood of reasonably affluent second- or third-generation Jews from Germany and Eastern Europe. In that setting intense discussions of capitalism, socialism, and communism, of the New Deal, the depression, and the threat of fascism, of orthodoxy and reformed Judiasm and atheism were commonplace. In other words, we grew up in a world of lively dialectic, to put a toney reference to it or Talmudic quibbling once removed, to give it its origin.

It was no surprise, then, that Nat the doctor, the analyst, and the institute director became a major challenger of stated doctrines. Nor were we surprised to hear him ask questions like, Is any prevailing view of schizophrenia acceptable in itself? Is the concept of the transference neurosis evolving or obsolete? Nor to hear him answering—against a prevailing trend—It is evolving. Nor to find him becoming interested in self psychology but soon asking, If empathy predominates, then where is the place for the worthy adversary?—and then telling a tale of the therapeutic effect on the transference of an episode of arm wrestling. Nor his challenging admonition that self in self psychology is as apt to become anthropomorphic as was ego in ego psychology.

Finally, I recall the heated phone calls we had about his insistence on using the word ludic in the title of his wonderful paper, “On Play Elements in Regression,” which began the first issue of Psychoanalytic Inquirty. Ludic, he said, emphasized a special, nonserious quality of the interactional context of a transference neurosis. Play, I said, played better to the readers we hoped to appeal to.

Vicissitudes of Gender Identity in the Female Therapist/Male Patient Dyad

Barbara Marcus PHD

Barbara Marcus

309 Edwards Street
New Haven, CT 06511

Barbara Marcus  

Central to conceptualizing the special issues in analytically oriented treatment of male patients by female therapists is an examination of differences between women and men in the process of gender-identity formation. Of particular importance are the generally greater fragility of masculine identification, the concomitantly greater rigidity of defenses on its behalf, and the psychological threat of regression to the boy's early identifications with the preoedipal mother, or, using Stoller's phrase, “protofemininity” (Stoller & Herdt, 1982), in the absence of a maternal object.

I am proposing that an understanding of these differences assists in formulating the therapeutic process broadly, as well as many of the transference/countertransference concerns identified in the sparse but provocative literature on the topic. This literature will be referred to selectively as it illuminates aspects of the therapeutic process in the treatment of a gender-dysphoric male.

Barbara Fibel Marcus is Assistant Clinical Professor, Department of Psychiatry, Yale University School of Medicine.

The Analyst's Ego

Eloise Agger D.S.W.

Eloise Agger

Suite 227 West
7315 Wisconsin Avenue
Bethesda, Maryland 20814

Eloise Agger  

If, as Freud suggested, the character of the ego is a precipitate of lost and abandoned objects, and the history of those object choices (1923, p. 29), then what happens to the analyst's ego over time as a consequence of his or her daily empathic introspections with patients as significant objects? Since we listen to our patients with affective as well as cognitive receptors, under similar behavioral constraints as they, we take in far more than we can process consciously. Even though we expect the analytic perceptual instrument to be well honed through training and personal analysis, and that technical neutrality will insure sufficient distance for objectivity and self-regulation, we may miss certain second and third level effects that reverberate and remain with us long after the analysand has departed from the couch. How then does the analyst's work affect the analyst? What does analyzing do to the analyst?

Each analyst arrives at his or her personal and professional maturity by a different subjective route. Each carries into the work a variety of institutional, philosophical, and personality imprints that may enrich or hinder creative investment. Despite all this, as Harry Stack Sullivan reminded us, “we are all much more simply human than otherwise, be we happy and successful, contented and detached, miserable and mentally disordered, or whatever” (1947, p. 16).

Dr. Agger is Adjunct Clinical Faculty, Catholic University of America School of Social Work, Washington, DC.

Epilogue

Eloise Agger D.S.W.

Eloise Agger

Eloise Agger  

In a commentary some years ago on what university teaching does to the teacher, Jacques Barzun observed “teaching is extremely hard work; it is the original brain-drain, being the continual readjustment of one's thought to another's, not to placate or even to persuade, but to strengthen and enlarge, and make more complex” (1968, p. 55). Even as professors tend to lecture and grade, mathematicians iterate and reiterate, might we, like Disraeli upon hearing of the death of Talleyrand, fall into wondering what he really intended? One analyst used to remark that he was never sure whether he spent his time “healing wounds or wounding heels.” Another consoled a supervisee overwhelmed by the horror of a patient's narrative, “Look, misery keeps us in business.” Kurt Eissler when asked whether he would like to include an additional commentary to his article in this issue on the aging analyst, declined graciously, noting that “If I write any more, it's liable to discourage other analysts from growing older.” One thing is clear, seasoning in this work and the passage of time do not dim that “therapeutic twinkle.” In 1938, Freud himself, discovering on his return to Vienna that the Germans, in a raid on the city, had ransacked his office, simply shrugged his shoulders and remarked, “I would never have taken so much for a single visit” (Méras, 1983). Paradox and the inevitable come to be accepted with a characteristic serenity.

Observing various analytic minds at work is reminiscent of brain researcher Sir Charles Sherrington's word picture of the brain: “It is as if the Milky Way entered upon some cosmic dance. Swiftly the brain becomes an enchanted loom where millions of flashing shuttles weave a dissolving pattern, always a meaningful pattern though never an abiding one: a shifting harmony of subpatterns” (Restak, 1984, p. 305). In the preceding essays we have witnessed further signs of the evolution of a new perspective in psychoanalytic work.

James Grotstein Issue Editor

James Grotstein

James Grotstein  

The theme of autism, once a remote entity associated with mental retardation, has captured the attention and imagination of infant-development researchers and clinicians in recent times. It has now come to have meaning in its own right for psychoanalytic study and treatment. Even more importantly, however, it demonstrates exaggerations as well as departures from more general primitive mental states that reveal significant parallels for higher order conditions. Frances Tustin, one of our contributors, for instance, speaks of “autistic enclaves in neurotic patients.”

We are privileged in this issue in having at our disposal an autobiographical account of secondary autism by an adult clinical psychologist, Ellen Stockdale, who generously shares with us what it has been like to be so different and how she viewed the world. (Dr. Andrea Moscowitz [personal communication] tells me that another autobiographical account of an autistic patient tallies in many ways with Ellen Stockdale's [see Grandin & Scariano, 1986].)

The Stockdale report was submitted to an international roster of psychoanalysts who are known for their interest in autism and their contributions to the literature on the subject. Their discussions of the report constitute the remainder of this issue of Psychoanalytic Inquiry.

The forerunners of the field of infant psychiatry that was ultimately to include autism took the form of such infant distress syndromes as “marasmus” (Spitz, 1945)

Supervising Female Therapists: A Comparison of Dynamics While Treating Male and Female Patients

Dale Mendell PHD

Dale Mendell

132 East 35th Street, #10F
New York, NY 10016

Dale Mendell  

Gender differences in psychoanalytic treatment and in dynamic psychotherapy have only recently become the focus of clinical research and exploration. A long-standing tradition within psychoanalysis asserts that the analyst's gender is of little importance because the patient replicates important transference configurations irrespective of it. Recently, however, a number of observers (Person, 1985a; Meyers, 1986; Moldawsky, 1986) have explored differences within the four possible gender dyads and have found that initial transferences, transference sequences, and the relative length and intensity of various transference manifestations are indeed influenced by the gender of the analyst.

This shift in the climate regarding gender and therapy opens the door to considering the effect of genders in the supervisory triad on the therapeutic process. Countertransference Strain and the Use of the Analyst

Elsa First MA

Elsa First

300 Central Park West
New York, NY 10024

Elsa First  

For many of us, our way of analytic listening has shifted over the last 15 years or so. We listen to the patient, but along with this we listen to the dialogue in the consulting room, to discern what kind of relationship is perhaps being enacted between the two participants. We hope to use this information to help us recognize patterns of transference and countertransference or “role responsiveness” (Sandler, 1976). But in all this, what are we to call real, actual, or illusory? Having come this far from a positivist opposition of transference versus reality, how are we to orient ourselves? As a contribution to making the ambiguities of this question discussable in clinical terms, I here present material from an analytic patient for whom, for a while, only the analyst's perceived failings were real.

I want to highlight a moment when the patient could begin to experience transference as partly his own subjective contribution rather than primarily trying to prove that the analyst is “really” recreating a failure of the object. Prior to this, the patient had been trying to establish how much the analyst contained unwanted aspects of the patient, or of the patient's defensive, masochistic, identifications with the failing object. I see this moment as an example of a turning point which occurs in some analyses, particularly with some traumatized patients who do not start treatment able to do ordinary analytic work.

Elsa First is a Training and Supervising Analyst, New York Freudian Society; she is on the faculty of the New York University Postdoctoral Program in Psychotherapy and Psychoanalysis.

Michelle Friedman  

The impact of a significant event in an analyst's life on the treatment process makes for compelling study, for it invites exploration of the boundaries of the analytic situation as it is influenced by the analyst's fluctuating internal dynamic state. The events affect the analyst's conscious and unconscious receptivity and hence the capacity to analyze. When such an event is repeated at a later stage of the analysis, it offers a rare opportunity to compare and contrast the patient's responses as potential indicators of change.

Pregnancy represents a unique intrusion into the analytic situation. Birth is a motif that evokes powerful primitive fantasies, fears, and longings in all persons. Careful as the analyst may be to preserve her anonymity, the pregnant state eventually becomes evident and provokes or intensifies transference, countertransference, and resistance reactions. Unlike illness, when the analyst can often minimize unnecessary disclosure in explaining absences and changed appearance, the pregnant analyst's condition inevitably becomes “public property” in the analysis.

Dr. Friedman is Assistant Clinical Professor of Psychiatry, Mt. Sinai Medical Center, and is Staff Psychoanalyst, Center for Psychoanalytic Training and Research, Columbia University.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Epilogue

James Grotstein Issue Editor

James Grotstein

James Grotstein  

Our contributors seem to vary with regard to their ideas about the etiology of autism, some regarding it principally as a constitutional or neurocognitive disorder and others suggesting that it is an early developmental deviation in the service of dealing with unmitigated terror where there is an intense fusion with mother and a lack of preparation for separation. The latter point of view does not exclude primary neurobiological considerations. The picture that seems to emerge is that autism is probably a biological disorder (genotype) intermixed with a psychological disorder (phenotype) in which there is a failure on the part of the infant to countenance separation, resulting in its entering into a default position whereby it regressively reinstitutes a primary autistic withdrawal and, at the same time, needing the environmental objects to be all the more “holding” and “containing,” but to such a degree that apparently a pathological relationship with the caretaking mother results, which can be characterized as “addictive.”

What is remarkable about the discussions is that each contributor found something in the report that corresponded with his or her own clinical experience. It might be necessary to put the etiology of autism on hold for a while, but the report itself throws considerable light on what lies behind the symptoms confronting the clinician.

If we have brought this elusive disorder closer to being understood, we can perhaps consider this issue of Psychoanalytic Inquiry to have advanced our knowledge to some degree.

When eva lester presented her paper, “The Female Analyst and the Erotized Transference,” at the meeting of the American Psychoanalytic Association in December, 1982, there was only one report in the literature describing an intensely erotic transference in a male patient with a female analyst (Bibring-Lehner, 1936). Didier Anzieu

7 Bis Rue Laromiguière

Didier Anzieu  

Ellen Stockdale's paper is very interesting thanks to both the abundance and the precision of the details she noted with regard to her disorder (secondary autism at the age of 28) as well as to the interaction between her psychotherapy and her activity as a healer of patients afflicted with primary autism. The patients have served her as a mirror through which she could learn to know herself. This learning process was especially important inasmuch as one of the problems she suffered from was her difficulty to mirror, as a response, the gestures, attitudes, and nonverbal behaviors of others.

Stockdale's observations were written from a cognitive point of view. She assumes that the ensemble of the observed facts accounts for our distortion of social perception, which, in its turn, is due to a congenital biogenetic defect. The patient says she concealed this distortion through a split in her personality. The distortion became manifest during a crisis precipitated by a double failure in love relationships, one hetero- and the other homosexual in nature. The cure is attributed to “learning processes” exercised by the therapist and colleagues at work.

My perspective is different. My approach is psychoanalytic.

M. Anzieu is Emeritus Professor of Psychology, Université de Paris, Nanterre; he is also Vice President of the Psychoanalytic Association of France.

Laila Karme  

Attention has been increasingly focused, in the last few years, on gender issues in the analytic situation. Evolution of concepts of transference and of gender development has gradually led to a nonpejorative — although still controversial — view that gender may indeed influence the analytic process without necessarily affecting the outcome (Kulish, 1984).

In focusing attention here on the female analyst-male patient dyad, I address two phenomena: First, the erotic transference in this dyad — and related countertransference issues; second, the extent to which paternal transferences develop — and related countertransference issues.

First the erotic transference: There seems to be an ongoing controversy over whether or not male patients develop erotic transferences toward their female analysts. The consensus here may be greater than is at first apparent. The question is really not whether male patients develop erotic transferences toward their female analysts — of course they do — but whether there are general differences in its manifestations, due to gender, in this particular dyad.

A paucity exists in the literature of reports of fully developed, sustained erotic transferences by male patients in analysis with female analysts.

Dr. Karme is on the Faculty at the Southern California Psychoanalytic Institute and is Clinical Associate Professor of Psychiatry, University of Southern California School of Medicine.

When I was a child, a psychoanalyst told me that most people become analysts to learn about themselves. I wasn't sure what he meant. Was it learning from books? Or by studying others? There is a particular terror that many male patients experience and often flee from as they approach feelings associated with the early maternal erotic transference. While preoedipal regression stirs degrees of anxiety in all men (Tyson, 1982b), the primal fear of intimacy experienced by schizoid males may provoke the terror of annihilation. In this paper, I review and integrate our understanding of the maternal erotic transference (Wrye & Welles, 1989) and the maternal erotic countertransference (Welles & Wrye, 1991) to illuminate the nature and implications of this “erotic terror” for male patients and their analysts. Brief clinical examples will illustrate a neurotic male's muted entry into shifting preoedipal and oedipal maternal erotic transference and compare and contrast this with the appearance of the maternal erotic transference and resistances to preoedipal erotic terror in a more disturbed male analysand.

Dr. Wrye, a Training and Supervising Analyst, is President of the Los Angeles Institute and Society for Psychoanalytic Studies (LAISPS) and a member of the International Psychoanalytical Association and Past President of Women and Psychoanalysis, Division 39. She is a member of the faculties of the Wright Institute Post Graduate Center in Los Angeles, and U.C.L.A. Extension.

This paper is presented under a single authorship, but it represents a synthesis of my own thinking and of my collaboration with Dr. Judith Welles of the Los Angeles Institute and Society for Psychoanalytic Studies.

While we would all agree that transference is of central importance to psychoanalytic treatment, it remains a matter of continuing controversy as to how much and in what ways the phenomena described with this term are to be attributed to present “reality” or to past “illusion.” In his earliest formulations, Freud tied these affective manifestations to the patient's past. However, this view—which in retrospect may be seen as covertly containing a distancing maneuver included for the comfort of the analyst—did not represent a satisfactory or definitive solution to all of the difficulties present. Ultimately, Freud developed a complex position: on the one hand, he continued to see transference feelings as “new editions” of old “facsimiles” (1905, p. 116); on the other hand, he not only acknowledged the actuality of these feelings, but saw them as an important tool for change within the treatment.

Countertransference is not the only possible determinant of an analyst's inept or erroneous responses, and surely not of his relevant responses to the patient. This is true whether countertransference is conceptualized in its classic sense, as interference with an orderly process or, more broadly, as a source of information about the patient. An analyst's difficulties or his ease and accuracy of functioning may also follow from his or her reality-oriented response to actual, generic, structural attributes of the transference itself. Traditionally, the analyst's role has been to make himself a neutral “blank screen” to facilitate the reenactment of past relationships within the present therapeutic context. Current thinking in psychoanalysis and psychotherapy has placed increased emphasis on the importance of the interaction between patient and therapist in the curative process (Gill, 1982). With this new emphasis has come a rejection of the idea that the analyst is a blank screen and increasing acceptance that real characteristics of the therapist, such as personality, race, and gender, inevitably enter into the therapeutic interaction.

At the same time, female writers have begun to raise questions about possible gender bias in the field of psychoanalysis, including the possible role of the analyst's gender in the therapeutic process. These two currents — from the interactionalists and from the femininists — both advance the supposition that the therapist's gender may be an important, though hitherto unacknowledged, factor in the course of therapy as transferences surface and are worked through.

Until recently, very little has been written on this subject.

Is Love in the Analytic Relationship “Real”?

Axel Hoffer MD

Axel Hoffer

14 Welland Road
Brookline, MA 02146

Axel Hoffer  

In his analysis of dora, Freud (1905, p. 116) wondered: “What are transferences?” His answer—“They are new editions or facsimiles”—raises questions highly relevant to recent shifts in psychoanalytic theory and technique. In what follows I consider three related questions:

Are positive transference and countertransference feelings imitations of true loving feelings or are they real?

What is the difference between a loving analytic relationship and an ordinary loving relationship?

What is the nature of the tension created in the analyst by the opposing tendencies of the relatively anonymous asymmetry in the analytic relationship and the self-revealing mutuality in an ordinary loving relationship?

Two quotations from Freud are immediately relevant: In discussing the analyst's response to the intense transference love of a female patient for a male analyst, he (1914) said: “It is, therefore, just as disastrous for the analysis if the patient's craving for love is gratified as if it is suppressed. The course the analyst must pursue is neither of these; it is one for which there is no model in real life” (p. 166). Two years later, in the context of neurotic symptom formation, Freud (1916-1917) wrote, “it is psychical reality which is the decisive kind” (p. 368).

Aradical shift occurred in the explanations given to the etiology of autism in the Seventies. Rimland (1964) and Ornitz and Ritvo (1976; Ritvo, 1976) challenged Kanner's (Kanner, 1942) view that the disorder was related to early maternal deprivation. They suggested an organic basis for the disorder. Mahler (1965; Mahler & Furer, 1968) also hypothesized a neurological basis for the disorder, but maintained that the disorder was treatable through a special form of intensive psychotherapy that involved the mother as well as the child. Only Bettleheim (1976) remained adamant that the disorder reflected the child's response to an environment that was experienced as uncaring and unresponsive. Similar questions were not raised regarding what Ellen Stockdale calls secondary autism, which we now diagnose, according to DSM III-R (1987), as a Specific Development Disorder, disorders that are presumed to have a neurological basis (Bryan & Bryan, 1986).

On Possible Effects of Aging on the Practice of Psychoanalysis: An Essay

K. Eissler MD

K. Eissler

300 Central Park West
New York, NY 10024

K. Eissler  

In a letter to max eitingon, Freud (1960) wrote that the decade between fifty and sixty was “the most beautiful and the richest in content” (p. 392) and was still to come for Eitingon. The occasion for this letter was the death of Eitingon's mother. Eitingon was then forty-nine years old and Freud seventy-three; his own mother, ailing because of old age, would die within half a year. The reason that the remark about the sixth decade found its way into a condolence letter to his friend and pupil can be reconstructed. In the same letter, preceding the comment in question, Freud confessed that his still-living mother “bars my way to the longed-for rest, to the eternal nothingness” (pp. 391-392). This statement demanded forceful proof that it had no validity for Eitingon, whose mother's death would otherwise similarly have opened the way to eternal nothingness for him. Therefore, Freud's praise of the sixth decade may have been more forceful than it would have been in different circumstances.

For Freud the sixth decade had been indeed blessed.

This article is a revised and expanded version of Eissler, K. R. (1975), Uber mogliche Wirkungen des altersprozesses auf die psychoanalytische Berufsausbung. Ein Essay. In: Die Beziehung zwischcn Arzt und Patient. Zur psychoanalytische Theorie & Praxis. Festschrift fur Wolfgang Loch zum sechzigsten Geburtstag, Sebastian Goeppert, ed. Muchen: List Verlag, pp. 109-121. The original paper was first published in Germany. It was translated by Dr. Ruth S. Eissler.

Ellen Stockdale's paper offers a moving account of the torments and burdens of the perceptual/emotional world of an autistic person. I was particularly fascinated by her description of the relentless echo effect of other people's voices and was led to wonder how this might link with the repetitive phrases and echolalia in autism. I am certain it has implications for therapeutic technique: how would such a person hear interpretations, and how might he or she be helped to reduce the echo effect? It would seem that something is wrong with the medium/space in which the sounds are traveling. Is it too vast, too empty?

It has been well documented that autistic people have difficulty in filtering and regulating their sensory and emotional experience (Tustin, 1981; Dawson and Lewy, 1989). It is either too close, or, as in the case of a very ill passive autistic patient of mine, Robbie, too remote and faint. Robbie's inner world was perpetually empty, and when an object appeared it seemed to have little to offer; he later called it a “net with a hole in it.” As he gradually came more to life and more into contact, one particular fantasy was central. He saw himself as down a deep pit but was able to come dramatically to life when someone threw him a very very long rope to pull him out.

Anne Alvarez is Principal Child Psychotherapist, Tavistock Clinic, London.

On Psychogenic Autism

Frances Tustin

Frances Tustin

17 Orchard Lane
Amersham, Bucks HP6 5AA
England

Frances Tustin  

Ellen Stockdale's autism became apparent when she was in her twenties. I wish to relate what she said about the onset of her autistic breakdown to what I have learned from psychotherapy with Kanner-type autistic children whose overall autism had been apparent from early infancy, often from birth. Ellen's autism had been associated with a split-off part of her personality that she characterized as “Red”. The “Ellen” part of her seems to have been what Winnicott (1958) has called “a caretaker self”. This “caretaker self” had enabled her, as she says, “to pass through the system” in a state of being “withdrawn, painfully shy, and lacking in confidence.” It was only when a series of events broke through this fragile façade that her autism was exposed.

Stockdale calls it “secondary autism.” The hypothesis of pathological autism being a regression to an early infantile stage of normal autism had been propagated by Mahler (1958) who, like myself (1991), abandoned it as infant observations by such workers as Stern (1985), Trevarthen (1979), and Miller et al. (1989) made the idea of normal autism in earliest infancy untenable. Grotstein's (1980) formulation of a “dual track” in early infancy in which undifferentiated states alternate with more differentiated ongoing ones is an attempt to incorporate these new findings concerning early infancy into our scheme of understanding.

Frances Tustin is Honorary Member, Association of Child Psychotherapists. She is also an Honorary Affiliate of the British Psychoanalytic Society.

I should like to present the case of pauline, who suffered from a symbiotic psychosis, and compare her with the remarkable presentation made by Ellen Stockdale. In my discussion I compare the stage of symbiotic psychosis, as demonstrated by Pauline, crossed by primitively encapsulated autistic children in the course of their evolution.

I shall try to elucidate the paradox between the constant search for the confusion of identities through massive destructive projective identification in the symbiotic psychosis, and through adhesive identity into autism with the fear of normal fusion. I approach this contradiction specifically through the vicissitudes of the formation of spatial relationships. I present some of my own hypotheses with regard to the formation of the body ego (body image) as it emerges with increasing precision in children afflicted by primary and secondary autism who are in analysis.

Martin Bergmann  

In a well-known letter written on September 21, 1897, Freud confided to Fliess that he no longer believed in his “neurotica.” He was referring, of course, to his seduction theory. Among the reasons he cites: “there are no indications of reality in the unconscious, so that one cannot distinguish between truth and fiction that has been cathected with affect” (Masson, 1985, p. 264). Since then the distinction between “psychical reality” and “material reality,” to use Freud's terms (1900, p. 620), remains central to psychoanalytic theory and technique.

In his last three papers written just a year before his death, Ernst Kris (1956a, b, c) challenged the clear-cut distinction between memories and fantasies. He outlined a major technical change by shifting his clinical emphasis away from the actual historical reality to the nature of the psychoanalytic hour itself. Kris argued that in a productive analysis every hour had its unique structure. Dreams, fantasies, memories, and current events, as well as transference reactions, were enlivened by the flow of the hour. Thus the hour had a reality of its own that was bound to affect the conceptualization of actuality and illusion.

Martin Bergmann is Clinical Professor of Psychology, New York University Postdoctoral Program in Psychoanalysis and Psychotherapy. He is a Training and Supervising Analyst at the New York Freudian Society.

Is there—or should there be drawn—a meaningful distinction between actuality and illusion in psychoanalytic theory and practice? At first glance, such a question may seem trivial. Our everyday common sense helps us to distinguish truth from distortion, reality from fantasy. However, as the various contributions to this issue have demonstrated, “truth” and “reality” in psychoanalysis are neither everyday nor common-sensical. The monumental discovery that led Freud to renounce his seduction theory was not the Oedipus complex per se, but rather his recognition of a realm of complex mental functioning in which unconscious fantasies join with historical events as major organizational determinants in the construction of individual experience, a realm he called “psychic reality.”

While enriching the scope and complexity of psychoanalytic theory, Freud's elevation of the concept of psychic reality to a central place in his theory introduced an epistemological dilemma with which current analytic theorists, including many of our contributors, continue to struggle. As noted in our introduction, “the separation of actuality and illusion is not as clearcut and straightforward as had been assumed.

Otto Weininger  

Peter, a three-year-old child, carried a piece of a darkly colored stone in his right hand as he entered my room. He came in with his mother, but as he walked through the door, it seemed that he had no sense that his mother was following so closely behind him. He neither glanced back toward her, nor did he look at me or the room. He seemed to “float” into my room; I had the strong impression that he was making it “his” room and that he had effectively blocked me out of his world. He looked at the ceiling, not at the floor or the walls. Then I became aware of the stone in his hand because he kept pushing it into his thigh as he moved. As he gazed vaguely around, he suddenly dropped down on his bottom as if his feet had given way from under him. He just “stopped,” and he looked terrified. I suggested to his mother that she might want to see if he was comfortable. Her response was, “Peter often does that. He looks about and then falls down. I don't know what to do.”

Peter seemed to be avoiding looking at me. I stopped trying to engage his glance and instead did two things. First, I said, “I think this room is not a safe room for you right now. I'll try to make it safe for you. When you and I are in this room, it will always be the same.” Second, I gently stroked his chest.

Dr. Weininger is Professor of Clinical Child Psychology in the Department of Applied Psychology at the Ontario Institute for Studies in Education, University of Toronto, Canada.

George Moraitis  

Freud's self analysis provided the data upon which the science of psychoanalysis was created. This highly original and exemplary approach to scholarly and scientific investigations has by and large not been pursued subsequently. The study of the analyst's contributions has instead been restricted to issues pertaining to countertransference, a term Freud himself introduced in 1910 (p. 144) in order to describe the unanalyzed aspects of the analyst's personality that interfere with his analytic work.

Contemporary authors, such as Giovacchini (1989), Loewald (1986), Racker (1968), and Winnicott (1949), have expanded the concept of countertransference to include aspects of the analyst's thoughts and feelings that are set in motion by the patient's transference communications, whether neurotic or not. This expansion has produced several competing theoretical and clinical conceptualizations that essentially examine the analyst's response as a reaction to the stimulus that the patient communicated to him. This one-sided exploration of a complex interaction between two autonomous individuals does not seem to take into account that the analyst does not simply react to his patient's communications; he also originates interactions by his presence and ideas that affect the analytic process. Furthermore, it is not only the patient who is affected by the analytic process, the analyst is affected as well.

Dr. Moraitis is a Training and Supervising Analyst, Chicago Institute for Psychoanalysis; he is also on the faculty at Northwestern University.

The concept of boundaries and distance in the analytic situation has been given little attention in the literature: distance not in the physical sense or, strictly, as an aspect of technical neutrality, but as a dimension of the affective interactions between patient and analyst. Distance is generally seen as the opposite of closeness, and both are understood to exist on a continuum from a hypothetical total intimacy and fusion, eliminating boundaries, to an equally hypothetical total isolation and absence of relatedness. Distance or closeness defines and reflects the fluctuations of affective tone in the analytic exchange—all analytic exchanges, verbal and nonverbal.

Bouvet focused specifically on the changes of distance between analyst and analysand and on the analysand's need to control boundaries and distance during analysis. In the pregenital and more primitive type of relating where symbolic displacements and expressions of undifferentiated emotions are common, the analyst, Bouvet believes, is experienced ambivalently, either as a good object to gratify all instinctual yearning or as the destructive, malevolent object threatening the integrity and cohesion of the patient's ego.

Ellen Stockdale's paper is a moving yet chilling account of terrible mental sufferings. When listening to some of our analysands from the other side of the couch or when observing the behavior of some of our child patients within the playroom, we perhaps seldom fully realize the all-pervasive extent of their pain. Particularly when working with very disturbed, so-called autistic or psychotic young children, it is often difficult to empathize fully with their sufferings as shown by their nonverbal behavior.

It is principally the account of the events and the emotions of Ellen Stockdale's early years that I find amazingly absent in this otherwise fascinating and complex paper. We know nothing of her family, its components, or the atmosphere filling it. We are just told that her life was seemingly “normal” til about the age of 28. From her account her pathology emerges as having little or no roots in her past. Yet we know that much of the pathology to be found in later life has in fact its roots in an often remote past.

As Hanna Segal has written, “We know that the fixation points of psychoses lie in the earliest months of infancy. Furthermore, we know that in psychological illness regression occurs, not to a phase of development that was in itself normal, but to one in which pathological disturbances were present, creating blocks to development and constituting fixation points (1964, p. 54).

In this paper I discuss some of the difficulties associated with the notion of a dichotomy between physical and psychic reality, and the way in which the analyst's judgment concerning the nature of either influences his choice of interpretation. After briefly offering an alternative approach based on the concept of different versions of the history of physical reality and of psychic reality, I present clinical material to illustrate how the analyst may make use of information of different kinds — derived from his knowledge of the patient's history, his observations in the session of her tone and manner of speaking, as well as the contents of her material, and particularly his experience of the atmosphere and nature of the relationship that is being lived out between himself and the patient. Rather than trying to determine the nature of the patient's psychic reality as distinct from the material reality, the analyst can recognize, as the session unfolds, different versions of reality and can begin to build up a picture of that version which is most clearly manifested in the consulting room at the time, and which is probably the most useful focus for our understanding and our interpretive efforts.

Diana Diamond  

Commenting on a review by W. S. Williams that praised Jane Eyre had it been written by a man and condemned it as “odious” if written by a woman, Charlotte Bronte wrote, “To such critics I would say, ‘To you I am neither a man nor a woman — I come before you as an author only. It is the sole standard by which you have the right to judge me — the sole ground on which I accept your judgment’” (Wise, 1932).

A (female) interviewer recently asked Natalia Ginzburg whether her friendship with Elsa Morante “… was different from her friendship with other … writers because they were both women: She looks impatient. ‘Of course not. A writer is a writer. You care about writing. It isn't men or women. I find these feminists very annoying, putting together these anthologies of women writers. As if there were a difference. You sit down, you write, you are not a woman or an Italian. You are a writer’” (1990).

If one substituted “analyst” for “writer” and “patients” for “critics” or “friends” in these quotations, they would express a wish wistfully held by most analysts: to work in an anonymity within which patients' transference would unfold with a freedom not encumbered by the awkward fact that the analyst is real.

Until about 20 years ago that wish was more than a wish: it was a belief, one that began to be eroded only with the publication, in 1961, of Leo Stone's landmark monograph, The Psychoanalytic Situation. Prior to that work, Freud's poetic image of the analyst as mirror had so hardened into dogma that the actuality of the analyst was regarded as irrelevant to the psychoanalytic process. Transference would assert its power to obscure the reality of the person of the analyst, who meanwhile would maintain analytic anonymity, refraining from mentioning any personal information to the patient.

Robbie Burns, from the poem “To A Louse,” 1786

No analyst is free from narcissistic vulnerability. From the viewpoint of self psychology and intersubjectivity, narcissistic vulnerability can be understood as the frustration of one or other of the analyst's selfobject needs for mirroring, idealization, or indeed any other of the ways in which the analyst utilizes his patient as selfobject. Each analyst has his own particular areas of narcissistic vulnerability. We each have an ideal image of ourself (conscious or unconscious), as well motivated, effective, kind, lovable, tolerant, patient, and so forth. When experience with a patient fails to affirm such qualities we may react defensively by withdrawal, anger, or in a variety of other ways. A significant part of the analyst's growth in therapeutic capacity, must be derived from gradually accruing knowledge and mastery of these personal sensitivities.

Fear of Fusion: Nonverbal Behavior in Secondary Autism

Ellen Stockdale-Wolfe

Ellen Stockdale-Wolfe

160 Claremont Avenue, #4B
New York, NY 10027

Ellen Stockdale-Wolfe  

Although much has been written about primary, or infantile, autism as described by Kanner (1942) and on schizophrenia, the literature contains little about secondary autism. Secondary autism is a syndrome of enormous social deficits resulting from cognitive and perceptual disabilities that stem from a biological abnormality in the filtering system and produce underarousal, overarousal, or both. A weak ego structure results in perceptual and cognitive abnormalities. The fragility of the ego structure makes closeness and intimacy difficult, even seemingly impossible in the beginning stage.

This is a story of my own experience of secondary autism. It is the story of Red (the pseudonym I used when I wrote the original version in graduate school). I hope it will be of help to therapists in their work with patients such as myself.

Red “survived” a “normal” childhood in “normal” schools through the graduate level and has since held a full-time professional position in a library. In junior high and high school, teachers thought she was withdrawn, painfully shy, and lacking in self-confidence, but they never recommended therapy to her parents. While in college and in graduate school studying special education, Red worked with children with primary autism.

Ellen Stockdale-Wolfe's report was submitted to Psychoanalytic Inquiry and to the discussants under the name of Ellen Stockdale, which is the name used throughout this issue.
